meta.title: The Same Seven Notes
meta.summary: A natural minor is C major read from its sixth degree — the same seven pitches, nothing added or removed.

spans.text: The notes of A natural minor are
A B C D E F G
. Not a sharp or a flat among them. It is the C major scale, note for note, just started somewhere else.
Write out C major:
C D E F G A B
. Count to its sixth note —
A
— and read from there, wrapping back around to the start once you run out:
A B C D E F G
. Same seven pitches, nothing added, nothing removed. This is called the
relative
relationship — A minor is C major's
relative minor
, and C major is A minor's
relative major
The distance between them is a rule you can reuse in any key: a major scale's relative minor starts three semitones — a minor third —
below
its root.
C
down three semitones is
A
. Every major key has one, and it always sits there.

rows.text: C D E F G A B
A B C D E F G

spans.text: Relative answers where are the notes — nothing more. It says nothing about why the two scales sound different, because they don't have different notes to sound different with.
If you've worked through
What the Letter Actually Names
, you already have every note in this pathway on the neck — that pathway is strongly recommended before this one, since this one leans on it throughout.

That's what makes this pathway cheap. The dots you already know from C major don't move. What changes is not the map but which dot the map is drawn around. Nothing in this chapter asks you to learn a new note — only to look at the familiar ones differently, and to get comfortable calling the sixth one home instead of the first.
Here's the two scales side by side. Same seven letters, rotated to a new starting point — watch the small degree label under each chip change even though the letters don't.
Play both. The chips hold the same seven letters in both cards, just rotated — the thing that actually changed is the row of small labels underneath:
against
. The second card names its own scale
"Natural minor — Aeolian"
— that's the app's own label, not a new term to learn.
Try it on the neck yourself in the
Scale Visualizer
: set the root to
A
and the scale to natural minor, and it's the same board as C major with a different note lit as home.

But the same-notes story has a hole in it. It cannot explain why A minor sounds different from C major, because as far as this derivation is concerned, they're not different — they're the same seven notes wearing a different label. Something else has to account for the sound, and it isn't going to come from comparing C major and A minor to each other, since they don't disagree about anything. It comes from comparing A minor to something that shares its root instead.
The second derivation
keeps the home in place and moves the notes instead.
Both names point at the same seven notes. This pathway says natural minor throughout, so that is the only one you need.
